utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness? But I think you would like to first make some submissions, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On a few matters. We are usually waiting a few seconds until the witness comes in. If I do understand that there were three items. If you would start with the first one and then we already asked the usher to bring the witness into the courtroom and then we may have heard the first one once the witness is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. And, Mr. Groome, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can take this opportunity to introduce the Chamber to Mr. Kweku Vanderpuye, who will be taking the next witness, Mr. Kingori. Your Honour, the first issue then that I would address would be with respect to P18. On Monday the Defence objected to the Prosecution's tendering of 65 ter 28052, which was then marked for identification as P18. It is a report of a meeting between each of the three army commanders held at the airport on the 11th of July, 1995. The meeting culminated in an agreement that was signed by Rasim Delic for the Bosnian army; Tihomir Blaskic for the HVO; and Ratko Mladic for the VRS. I do not believe its relevance is contested, simply whether it meets the legal standard required for an exhibit to be considered an associated exhibit. The Chamber asked me to address where in P1, Mr. Harland's statement, this document was dealt with and why it is the Prosecution's position that it is an exhibit which is associated to that statement. Your Honours, both the Prosecution and Defence when calling a witness pursuant to 92 ter may seek to admit exhibits associated to that written evidence. This is well established in the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. This body of jurisprudence stands for the proposition that an exhibit which is an inseparable and indispensable part of the witness's written evidence is an associated exhibit, and such a test is met if the witness discusses the document in his or her written statement or transcript and if that written statement or transcript would have less probative value without its admission. This report and agreement are the subject of three paragraphs in P1, paragraphs 160 to 162. And if Your Honours would like to look at those paragraphs, they can be found on e-court page 48 of the original and 33 of the translation of Mr. Harland's statement. Mr. Harland describes the signing of the agreement at the airport on the 11th of January in -- and very briefly summarises the basic terms of the agreement. He goes on to say that the agreement was not in fact implemented, attributing it to "all three sides clearly had other plans." Also relevant to the Chamber's consideration of this issue is Mr. Lukic's query on cross-examination regarding this document, and that can be found at transcript page 834. Your Honours, the Prosecution's position is that the statement of Mr. Harland has less probative value for the Chamber if the Chamber does not have the benefit of the agreement itself. Mr. Harland only summarises the document to the extent necessary to discuss it in his statement. The Chamber should not substitute the original text agreed and signed by the accused and other significant persons relevant to this case with Mr. Harland's summary. The agreement itself is the best evidence of what is contained within that agreement and what Mr. Mladic assented to by his signature. It is for these reasons the Prosecution submits that P18 meets the legal test for admission as an exhibit associated to P1, Mr. Harland's statement. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Mr. Lukic, a response -- perhaps you prefer to briefly think it over. I see the witness is not in yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My problem is that I cannot find the document under that number. It's not an agreement what I can find in our e-court so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then that seems to be a very technical problem. I take it that the Prosecution will assist you in -- or whomever else will assist you to find the document and then you'll have an opportunity to respond at a later moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kingori, I take it. Before you give evidence, the Rules require you to make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kingori. Please be seated. Mr. Kingori, you'll first be examined by Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Vanderpuye is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Vanderpuye, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you, Your Honours. Good morning to Mr. Lukic, Mr. Stojanovic, Mr. Petrusic, and General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good morning to you, Colonel Kingori.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I know you've been here before, so I'm going to ask you or, rather, remind you to try and speak a little more slowly than you would otherwise so the interprets have a chance to keep up with us and interpret what you say and what I say accurately to the parties. And if you have any questions about what I ask you or require any clarification, don't hesitate to let me know and I'll do my best to do so. Let me get started with this. Do you recall having provided a witness statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on 8 January 2012, a so-called amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And this amalgamated statement, was it a document that essentially consolidated your prior testimonies in the case of Krstic from 31 March and 3 April 2000; Popovic from 12 through 14 December 2007; and the Tolimir case from 14 through 16 and the 20th of September 2010?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could please have 65 ter 28117 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Mr. Kingori?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber what it is?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: This is my amalgamated statement that I made during these previous trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could go to, please, page 49 in e-court -- rather, the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like you to take a look at that. Do you recognise the signature indicated here?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is that the date, 8 January 2012, the date which you signed this document?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, have you had an opportunity to review this amalgamated statement before coming here today since your testimony in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I had the honour to go through it on Sunday and Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Having had an opportunity to review your amalgamated statement, Colonel, does it fairly and accurately reflect what you would say were you to be examined here today and asked the same questions concerning the issues discussed in it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It reflects what I had said, and given the same situation I would say the same things again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I would tender the amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, there's one missing link. You haven't asked the witness whether he -- when he gave that statement that he gave that statement in accordance with the truth. Because if he would have said the same at the time and now says the same, we still have to know whether that's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President and I was referring -- you're right. But I can see that it's in the acknowledgement in e-court before the Chamber but I'll ask the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you gave the statement at the time fully in accordance with the truth as best as your recollection could --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It doesn't come as a surprise, but that makes the chain complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any objection against admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28117 becomes Exhibit P34, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P34 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before I make -- before I tender the associated exhibits I'd like to ask a few questions, but initially I'd like to read a brief summary of the witness's statement, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: From March to July 1995 Colonel Kingori was deployed to Srebrenica as a United Nations military observer. His unit was responsible for monitoring the VRS - ABiH cease-fire agreement and reporting violations as concerned the Srebrenica enclave. They also liaised with the conflicting parties and assisted international agencies operating within the enclave, such as UNPROFOR, IOM, and MSF. Kingori's main contacts with the VRS were with Major Nikolic and with Colonel Vukovic. While deployed to Srebrenica, Colonel Kingori observed the shortage of food and scarcity of reliable water and electricity supplies and that some of these shortages were due to VRS restrictions of aid convoys. Well before the July 1995 attack, Colonel Kingori noted the VRS presence deep inside parts of the enclave. VRS troops prevented the UNMOs' attempts to monitor the situation towards the separation line. Kingori was one of two UNMOs present in Srebrenica during the VRS attack precipitating its fall. He observed the heavy shelling of the enclave, which commenced on 6 July and intensifying over several days. If I need to slow down, please let me know. Kingori patrolled the town to assess the shelling damage and filed reports from the UNMO bunker in the Srebrenica PTT building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On 9 July, as the VRS encircled the enclave, the UNMOs were forced to leave Srebrenica town to Potocari for their safety. As the shelling continued in the days that followed, Srebrenica's population streamed into Potocari, seeking refuge and UNPROFOR's protection. By the end of 11 July, Muslim civilians filled the DutchBat compound at Potocari with others outside its perimeter. On 12 July, Colonel Kingori estimated approximately 30.000 refugees in Potocari. As VRS soldiers arrived and took up positions, Kingori went out to investigate. He encountered General Mladic near the compound with whom he briefly conversed. Mladic said that the VRS would provide buses for the evacuation of the refugees. Almost immediately thereafter buses arrived and VRS soldiers began making women and children board them. In the presence of senior VRS officers Kingori saw men and boys ages 14, 15, and 16 years old separated from their families and taken to the white house nearby. Colonel Kingori later approached Mladic with concerns about the poor conditions of their detention. Mladic disagreed and eventually accompanied Kingori to the white house. Nevertheless, he refused Kingori's request to enter. The men and boys were later removed from the white house without their belongings, including their identifications, and put on separate buses from those transporting the women and children. Although Colonel Kingori successfully prevented some younger boys from being placed on those buses, the VRS soldiers invariably forced more back on. His efforts to record the names of men to be transported by having them call out their names similarly proved difficult. On 13 July, the VRS continued to remove refugees from Potocari. Colonel Kingori accompanied MSF staff to evacuate patients from Srebrenica hospital to Potocari. Although some expressed their desire to remain at the hospital, VRS soldiers warned Kingori that if the patients were not removed they would be killed. By 14 July, only the wounded and staff remained. UNMOs helped MSF prepare a list of wounded, local staff, and interpreters to try to ensure their safe evacuation. This was negotiated during a meeting involving the UNMOs, DutchBat, MSF, ICRC, and the VRS, represented by Colonel Djurdjic, whom Kingori described as a senior officer with whom he met on other occasions. Professor Koljevic was also contacted concerning the matter. A few days later Colonel Kingori left Srebrenica with his unit together with DutchBat. That concludes my summary, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have a number of questions for Mr. Kingori, as you might anticipate. However, I do not intend to lead evidence to any degree of particularity that have been covered extensively by the adjudicated facts, in particular regarding the take-over which are facts numbered 1363 through 1388. There are a number of facts that overlap, obviously, that are relative to the narrative, particularly as concerns the accused's acts and conduct. In addition, there are facts I will not lead concerning the condition of the crowd at Potocari, although there is video footage I will cover with the witness. Similarly, there are certain facts concerning the separations that occurred, the organisation of the buses to remove the children, and some events concerning their removal and the incident charged at Schedule E 14.2 at Potocari. I won't cover all of his evidence regarding that, but again some issues will -- are necessary relative to the narrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori -- I'm sorry, Colonel Kingori, can you tell us since your last testimony before the Tribunal in January what you've been engaged in professionally.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, after my testimony here in January, I was engaged by the UN OCHA Somalia as an expert on civil military co-ordination on the war that is going on in Somalia. So I'm a consultant for them at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you just tell us in the briefest of terms what you do in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do co-ordinate issues to do with the Kenya defence forces, the AMISOM or the African Mission in Somalia, and also the humanitarian activities that are going on in Somalia though they are based in Nairobi. And also, I do train the officers who are going to be deployed -- the Kenyan officers who are going to be deployed in Somalia and also the humanitarian actors who are going to do their work in Somalia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to focus for a moment on your training prior to your deployment in Srebrenica, and specifically can you tell us first did you receive any training prior to your deployment as a UN military observer?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we got deployed to former Yugoslavia we got some training in Kenya on the historical background of the war, the geographical location, and the kind of weapons that we are bound to encounter when we get there and our roles as UN military observers. In addition, when we went to the mission area, we were briefed in Zagreb and did also a bit of training on the same things. And now, more specifically, with the weapons systems, the historical background of the war, when it started, the reasons why it started, and where the UN would like to take the country to, that is, to the end of the war and so that people can be able to live again in harmony.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you receive any training with respect to technical aspects of your work as a UN military observer?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We did some specific training. Part of it was on first aid. The other part was on the way to do greater analysis in case of any analysing that may come up in the course of our duty, identification of weapons and their ranges -- the effective ranges and the type, how they look like, and especially that the weapons systems were deployed there were different from the ones we were used to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you provided with any materials in order to facilitate your work in this technical aspect?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We were provided with some technical materials like calipers, measuring equipment, and also books to help us to refer to in case we encountered a certain weapon that we did not know the technical details of.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I'd like to ask you a couple questions, if I may, about the reporting that you did while you were deployed. Was there a protocol in place governing the types of reports, the number of reports, or frequency of reports concerning your unit?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there was. We were to prepare reports at the end of every day which we used to call situation reports, or sitreps in short, and they were prepared by 1800 hours to cover the last 24 hours. But on regular intervals, if anything happened in between we could update and call the situation report as update of the situation report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of the content of these situation reports, was there anything specifically required to be included in them?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there was several issues that we had to include. That one of them being the time we are reporting, that is, the date/time group; from where that report is coming from; and also to whom that we are sending the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was there a requirement that the information contained in the report -- or rather, the reported information be noted down close in time to the events that are the subject of the report?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't get the question clearly. If you can repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How close in time to the events that are reported in any given report were they? In other words, from the time of an event happening to the time that the report is made of it, how much time elapsed on a -- in a general sense, in a regular context?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had to make reports as soon as possible and at least not later than 24 hours otherwise it would be stale. So we had to give the reports as the events occurred, and as I said if it is after the 1800 hours, we had to give it as an update of the sitrep.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, have you checked whether there's any dispute about what you're now eliciting as evidence, that's the structure of reporting on a daily basis, et cetera? Have you checked whether the --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- with the Defence whether it's in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I haven't checked with the Defence whether it's in dispute. I understand, however, that the Defence doesn't have an objection to the associated exhibits. So to that extent, I am eliciting this information because I think it is relevant to and important to the admissibility of the associated exhibits. But to the extent the Defence doesn't object, and if the Chamber doesn't feel it's necessary, I won't persist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if there's no dispute about the structure of the reporting - and I'm looking at the Defence -I'm not talking about the content of the reports, that's, of course, a totally different matter, then I wonder whether -- and, by the way, I take it that we'll see all these reports appearing twice a day or, et cetera, so it's more or less self-explanatory. If there's no dispute about it, then I would tell us about what there's no dispute and then we could move on. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the way in which reports were being sent is not something that is in dispute as far as the Defence is concerned. It is the content that is in dispute, and I assume that both the Prosecutor and I will be dealing with that through our questions that will follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I take it there must be one way or another to put on the record that these matters, that's the structure of the reporting and apparently the scenarios developed for the reporting are not in dispute and what they were, that's twice a day, et cetera, instead of spending a lot of time on it in court. This is also an observation I make for future witnesses but of course also in relation to this witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There is just one other matter in light of what my colleague has expressed. To the extent that the content of the report is in dispute, that is, I assume the reliability of the information contained in the report, I do think it is necessary in that circumstance, then, to lead the evidence indicating why the reports are reliable or otherwise accurate and that's the reason why I'm asking these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I already clearly indicated that I make a distinction between the structure of the reporting system and the content of the report. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, with respect to the content of the report, as we've been discussing, can you tell us whether it was necessary for the reports to be accurate or reliable in any given circumstance, or how important was that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reports that we were giving had to be as accurate as possible, given the fact that the military observers were the eyes and ears of the UN on the ground and the information we were giving could be used by the other or the higher systems in the UN to take any action.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the information that was contained in the reports, was this limited to information that was directly observed by military observers or did it contain other information from other sources?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the information that we were giving contained what we observed as military observers and also what we went through during the meetings that we were holding with the warring factions and also any other information that we could get from outside. But I hasten to add that information that we were not confirming ourselves, we had to indicate that it was not confirmed by UNMOs and therefore write NCBU.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, is there anything which I have not read yet in paragraph 12 of the statement you asked about? There's no need to repeat what is already in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In paragraph 12 in particular, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. NCBU is, I think, the last part of that accuracy of the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's all there. Would you please focus on matters which you have not yet found or which really need clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what sources of information you relied on in particular in the reporting process.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the sources of information, as I've indicated, was what we could see ourselves, what we could discuss with either faction, and also what we could be told by anybody within the enclave or from the UN system that they may have wanted us to clarify on ground. Those are the main sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say sources from the UN system, did you rely on information from DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It involved the DutchBat, UNHCR, the UNMO headquarters, any other source that is concerned with the UN or UN humanitarian actors on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Would that include MSF?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And would it include sources from the -- from within the enclave, civilian Muslim sources?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And all of these, were they specifically indicated in the reports?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt. I just ask a question. Mr. Kingori, did your sources, so far as civilians were concerned, only concern Muslims or other ethnic groups as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's good to clarify that. We were living in the enclave where the Muslims were living. So mainly the source from there would be from the Muslims, but in case we went out to meet senior people like Major Nikolic who were Serbs, we could get information from them and still use it. But the predominant people in the enclave were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said "predominant," so you did also consult Serb civilians to a lesser degree? Is that -- should I understand predominant to mean that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The other group that was there was mainly the military element of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would at this time tender the associated exhibits. They're indicated in the exhibit list that we provided earlier. There is -- there are two documents that I have mislabelled inadvertently to add to those documents as associated, and those are 65 ters 4469 and 4471, refer to paragraphs 210 and 215 in the statement respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, would you like to respond now or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later at any rate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will deal with the associated exhibits soon afterwards. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, in your statement you say at paragraph 9 -- we could go to e-court, it's P34, although there may not be any need for it, it's P34, page 3 in the English, page 4 in the B/C/S. And I'll just read the section to you because I think it may be quicker. You state at paragraph 9: "At times they could tell us," referring to DutchBat, "if there was anything they want us to go and investigate, they could ask us to go and investigate a specific case, but not general."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are we at page 3 in the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you see that in the last sentence of the paragraph, Colonel, what I've just read to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what you meant, first of all, by a specific case and not by a general case or not in general?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: What I meant here is that the DutchBat -- I mean, we could use information from anywhere and DutchBat could also tell us in some instances that there were some specific cases they would like us to go and investigate, like maybe there was shelling in such and such a place and they would tell us to go and investigate. Also, they could give us information on the intrusion of the BSA inside the enclave, and they would request us to go and talk to the BSA leadership, that is, Major Nikolic and others; or just go there and investigate ourselves so that we can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What types of things are we talking about in terms of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Here we are talking about military incursions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Also the penetration of the BSA inside the enclave, mainly those were the issues, and also artillery shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you co-operate with other UN agencies operating in the area in a similar way or NGOs and so forth?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We were taking everything seriously. Whatever information we could get from any organisation or individuals, we were taking seriously and going ahead and investigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At paragraph 39 of your statement - and that's going to be at pages 9 in the English and pages 12 through 13 in the B/C/S - you say that you had certain information about planned UNHCR food deliveries, in part because of your responsibility to provide security for them during transit. I wondered, first of all, the type of information that you had, what was the source of the information concerning UNHCR food deliveries?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was a UNHCR presence in the enclave; they had offices there and their warehouses. And they used to talk to us, and in particular when they were going to -- they had plans to bring in food or other associated items, they would talk to us, request that we talk to the BSA so that they can allow the food in, and also at least know what they were doing for the people of the enclave because that was part of our mandate, to check the humanitarian and food situation in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me focus just a little bit about the -- on the humanitarian situation in the enclave. In your statement at paragraph 63, that's English page 15, B/C/S page 21, you refer to the occurrence of shelling in Srebrenica as a norm. And what I'd like to know - I think we can see it there in the middle of the paragraph - what I'd like to know in particular is: What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I meant was that shelling in Srebrenica was normal to a certain extent. Also small arms fire, machine-gun fire, that was normal. It was nothing serious. I mean, to us we knew it could happen any time and we were used to it; everybody was used to it. But this particular one was a bit too heavy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This particular one you're referring to, the attack on 6th July, 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm referring to that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the shelling that you refer to as the norm in Srebrenica, is that during the period throughout the period of your tenure there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. During my stay there, the shelling or the small arms fire was normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Originating from where, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, shelling was mainly incoming, meaning it was coming from the BSA side into the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 57 of your amalgamated statement, that's English page 14, B/C/S page 19, you indicate there that there were a lot of complaints about shelling or attacks into the enclave. How frequently would you say that these sorts of complaints were brought to your attention?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Which paragraph did you say, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you'll see it in the second sentence. It says: "In fact, we could not stay for long without some complaints coming from the Muslim concerning an attack somewhere."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What I meant here is that there were always complaints coming from the Muslims that a certain area had been shelled, a certain area, there were some people had been injured, or that they suspect the BSA are trying to penetrate from a certain area, they have taken a certain OP and there is an incursion there. All those complaints used to come to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you receive information as to what kinds of areas or places were targeted by the shelling during this period of time or in this context?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There were some areas which had high concentration of shelling, and especially from the southern side and also towards the Bandera Triangle. And we could even identify where the shelling was actually originating from.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what were you able to conclude based upon your ability to identify the origin of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only thing we could do at that particular time was to report to the UN system - that is the higher echelon - on what was happening, that is, on the -- on where the source could be after doing the crater analysis and also analysing the situation on ground to give them the appropriate areas, that is, in grid reference form or grid square, depending on the area so that they can be able to do whatever they wanted, that is, in case they wanted to do an air attack or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At paragraph 35 of your statement you indicate that there was never enough food in Srebrenica, and that's English page 8, B/C/S page 11. First of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- did you consider the answer given by the witness an answer to the question: What were you able to conclude based upon your ability? Do you consider it an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do consider it an answer, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thought the question - but perhaps I misunderstood your question - that you'd like to know what conclusions the witness drew from what they found on the ground. Of course to say: Well, the shell fell here or there. But I think it is mainly about the origin of the shells. And he said: Well, we reported what we knew about the origin. I understood your question to be what did you find about the origin of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would be happy to clarify that. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. If you didn't intend to ask it then -- but that's how I understood the question. But if you're satisfied with the answer, then please proceed as you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or maybe so I can clarify a bit --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- of the same?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if Mr. Vanderpuye is inviting you to do so. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Indeed I am. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What I meant is that we were able to conclude that the shelling was coming from the BSA side, that is what I meant; and the particular grid area, the grid reference or the grid square from where it could have been coming from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I may have been in the process of referring you to paragraph 35 of your statement, where you indicate that there was never enough food in Srebrenica. First, can you tell us what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, during my stay in Srebrenica, we could see that the people were never with enough food. They were mainly dependent on UNHCR supplies, but of course we know there were other sources of supply of food through the unofficial routes to Zepa and back. But mainly the inhabitants of the enclave were dependent on UNHCR food. This food was brought in on a schedule -- as scheduled and sometimes there were delays due to various reasons. So when those delays were there, obviously we could see the people are going hungry, and we know for sure they were unable to grow their own food that was enough to feed the enclave. That is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you apprised of the -- now, you've indicated that these -- the food was brought in on scheduled -- scheduled convoys, as it were. And were you apprised of the movement of these convoys, specifically?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were all informed about the schedule. First of all, to make sure that we seek clearance for the convoy to bring in the food, that is, from the BSA side; and also so that we can prepare the people to receive the food; and also for our reports because we had to indicate the availability of food for the people of the enclave in our reports. So that was the main reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to focus, if I could, on what you experienced -- your unit experienced, rather, with respect to the rotation of personnel, equipment, and supplies. Could you tell us very briefly about that. At paragraph 8 in your statement you say that: "Somewhere after April the BSA started denying the UNMOs permission to leave the enclave. Later on they allowed them to go out and upon their exit they said they cannot come back to replace them." That's paragraph 8, English page 3, B/C/S page 4. Now, with respect to the rotation of troops and the inability to replenish or replace personnel, were you provided with an explanation as to why troops, or rather, members of your unit going out couldn't come back?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, for any of our troops, and especially UNMOs, to leave the enclave or even to come in, permission had to be sought from the BSA so that they give written consent or approval that they allow this person or these persons to come in or to get out. And it was a tedious process because we had to apply, takes about one week, one month, sometimes they declined completely. And in this particular case there are some people who were to go on leave and they were denied permission to go. Let alone that leave was accumulated and it reached a situation where they were going and get replaced. They were still denied replacement, so when the three went there were no replacements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, sorry to interrupt you. The question was whether any reasons were given. You described the rotation and the denial of the people to come back. But the question was the reasons given to you not allowing new people to come in. Were any reasons given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are times they could give reasons like -- and that is what I was getting to - there were times they could not give any reason at all. Some of the reasons they were giving, and especially when we want -- we had been told to remain in the enclave, they said they cannot trust those who are coming in because they don't know them. In other circumstances they could not give any reason at all. They just said, No, we cannot allow you to come in or go out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were there any restrictions on the supplies that you had, that is, your unit had, placed -- imposed, rather, by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Our supplies were coming mainly through the DutchBat, and there are times they could get restrictions on resupply. And so we also get some problems -- we were getting some problems when there were restrictions on the resupply of DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What kind of supplies are you referring to? Is this equipment? Is this food?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was mainly food and diesel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What was the impact on your ability to carry out your work, given those restrictions?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, especially on the supply of diesel, it was a major predicament in that without diesel we could not be able to patrol the enclave, we could also not be able to run the generators to use -- to enable us to use the computers to send and receive reports and so it was a major headache. But on the side of food, obviously, without food we could not be able to work well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you bring this to the attention of the VRS personnel that you were dealing with throughout your tenure in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we did, and especially through Major Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you provided with any explanation with respect to the restrictions imposed on your supplies?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, he was always telling us that he's going to check with the higher commanders of the BSA and then inform us of the outcome, but most of the time it was never forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you consider the restrictions that were imposed on your supplies or the rotation of your personnel in your unit justified?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, those restrictions were not justified because we were there to work for the people inside the enclave. We were employed by the UN system and therefore there is -- could be no reason for them to restrict us at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to refer you to the attack - and I'm just going to ask a few questions about that if I may. In paragraph 67 of your statement, that's English page 16, B/C/S pages 21 through 22, you indicate that the shelling of Srebrenica, and this is during the course of the attack itself, followed a pattern. First, can you tell the Chamber what you meant by that, by this pattern as you describe it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the pattern that I'm referring to here was that we found after the BSA fired about a few shells, that is, around 20, 30, 50, or whatever over a given period of time, they could stop and wait for another 20, 30 minutes or so before the next shelling. So that's the period I'm referring to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did the shelling that occurred throughout the attack at Srebrenica, beginning on the 6th of July as indicated in your statement, follow a pattern or system with respect to the areas that were being shelled?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you explain that, Colonel, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: The shelling, and especially in Srebrenica town itself, it was following a certain pattern in that they could shell, then stop, then shell again. And what we felt and what we suspected was that maybe they were waiting for people after shelling to come out and pick the injured and the dead, and then when they are inside there where they had aimed earlier, they can still shell again the same place and kill more people, and it is -- it was in our reports and that is what I indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of the areas targeted, at paragraph 73 of your statement you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the Chamber wondered for the last questions what you elicited as evidence which we had not yet read in paragraphs 66 and 67. We read the statement. There's no need to elicit again the same evidence, and I -- really, I did not hear one word which was new after I had read paragraphs 66 and 67. Would you please keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you are now at paragraph 73 I think. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I was actually trying to elicit evidence concerning the pattern of shelling separately than the timing of the shelling itself, just for your information so that you don't get the impression that I'm trying to elicit the exact same evidence that's in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then put your questions in such a clear way that we do not finally receive the same evidence as we have read before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And emphasize that it's about areas and not about timing that you are asking questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, I refer you to paragraph 73 of your statement, that's English page 17, I believe, B/C/S page 23, where you say: "The way the shelling was done was definitely aimed at the residents of that place." And what I'd like to know is how you draw that particular conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: I'm looking for the sentence, Your Honour. Para 73.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The very first sentence, Mr. Kingori.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can find it. What I meant here is that the targeting of the enclave, and especially the areas where you would expect more people, like the market, and also some other socio areas, that is what I meant when I said that it was definitely aimed at the residents of that place. They were also targeting the residential areas, the market and all those areas, so I believed - and we had reason to believe - that they were targeting the civilians of that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were those areas, to your knowledge, militarised in any way?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were living in that enclave. We had reason to believe that there were no military targets because there were no barracks inside there that we could see, there were no major equipments put anywhere, and there were no military people that we could see in that -- in those particular targeted areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to focus, if I could now, on the 12th and 13th of July. Beginning on the 12th, did you -- first of all, do you remember that day in particular and where you were?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I remember I was in -- we were in Potocari at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you meet General Mladic on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It -- I was very pleased to meet General Mladic, the very senior person in charge of the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Where did you meet him, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was in Potocari outside the DutchBat, near where the bulk of the IDPs were placed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just for the record, could you clarify what you mean by "IDPs"?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: That is the internally displaced persons who had come all the way from other villages in the enclave to Potocari. And just to clarify that some of them stayed inside DutchBat and others stayed outside in the open. And where the General was, General Mladic was actually in the outside area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And you had an opportunity to speak to General Mladic in that context?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was pleased to talk to him, but initially when he recognised my patch, reading "Kenya," we started some informal discussion about where I come from, athletics and all those things, before I started informing him through interpreters about other situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a little bit of video footage, if I may. It's 65 ter 26123. And we're going to start with V0009035, and we should start at 17.57.4 and hopefully play it through 19.03. I'd like you to just take a look at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. We've stopped at 19.04.09.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First, Colonel, do you recognise the area that's shown in this video footage?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what do you recognise it at?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: This was the area outside DutchBat, slightly towards Srebrenica town. As you leave from Potocari on the -- the first part was on the left side as you go up, and currently what is being shown here is -- was on the right as you go towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is this the area approximately in which you met General Mladic on the 12th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the general area that I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could we just play from 20.41 through 20.1 [sic]. Okay. We can go ahead and play this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the record, we've stopped at 21.10 -- sorry, .6. And I misspoke on the record, I intended and indicated to play from 20.41 through 21.1. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recognise what's transpiring in this particular footage, Mr. -- Colonel Kingori?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do, and I can tell you that this -- what the BSA soldiers trying to give some food, and especially in the last one that you showed, some biscuits, some candies to the IDPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what happened with respect to that -- those biscuits and candies later on?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, immediately the BSA gave out these candies, there would be a spell whereby the videoing would be going on; and then after that when the video is not focused on that particular area, they would go back and pick the candies, something which some of us could not understand why they were doing that. Why give the kids candies and later on pick them from them? It didn't make sense to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the individual that was depicted in this particular clip?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, I could -- I can remember him. It's only that the name right now is gone. But he's someone I know. I've talked about him before. But it's a long time. I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we go to 23.58 and play that hopefully through 25.20.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. We've stopped at 24.22.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the people in this frame?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do. There are two, I think, important people here. To the right there is General Ratko Mladic and at the far corner you can see a very black person there. I think that is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. You think or you know?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: I am sure that is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue playing, please, through 25.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, before you ask any questions, does the Prosecution intend to rely on the text as we -- it's -- which is apparently spoken and translated into English on the screen? If that is the case, if you would not -- us to ignore it, then it should be on the transcript, and it should be on the transcript in French as well, and you should have provided transcripts of this video to the booth so that they could have followed and translated what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry, Mr. President. I believe that we do have transcripts of this trial video. I'm not sure if it's of all the words that are spoken or just the subtitles, which I will check. And my understanding is that we have given -- first of all, we have obviously disclosed this to the accused. I don't believe that we provided that, however, to the booths to the extent that the subtitles are clear on the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which means that we have an incomplete record of what was said here, especially, for example, that there is no French, and at least on the transcript we cannot read what was said on this video and that may be relevant, so therefore we'll have to find a solution for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome most likely will be able to inform you about how I have instructed the Prosecution in previous cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll discuss that with Mr. Groome at my earliest opportunity. I wasn't aware that there was a particular protocol with respect to the -- with respect to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- presenting this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Inform yourself through Mr. Groome and then let's see whether we can agree on that. That might be relevant for the Defence at a certain stage as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. We'll have to play this through 25.2 -- I'm sorry, .20.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, I just have a couple of questions regarding this clip. At the beginning of the clip you can see General Mladic discussing something concerning the boarding of the buses or the transport of the people. Do you recall that conversation in general?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is that reflected in your statement concerning General Mladic talking about the buses and the transport of the individuals at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It is in my statement is so explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that about the time or close in time to the conversations that you had with General Mladic concerning your having been from Kenya or from the Kenyan armed forces?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was after that and that's the time I explained to him that the UN was preparing transport, and he said no he has his own transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the latter part of the clip in which General Mladic is talking to members of the crowd and assuring them that they will be safe and that no one will harm them, were you there during the course of this particular transaction that we see now in the monitors?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was close by. I was just there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what was your assessment of the situation concerning this group of civilians that were gathered there to be transported out? Did it -- was it consistent with what General Mladic was saying or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, General Mladic was just doing the right thing at that particular moment, trying to cool the tempers of the people, trying to show them that nothing bad will happen to them, that they should have some hope, to pre-empt maybe a scenario whereby they would protest or demonstrate or do something that would be bad. So I think he was doing the right thing to cool them down and also tell them that they will be safe on their way out, which actually is an assurance that he was not obliged to obey.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did that agree with your assessment of what was happening at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you say at paragraph 30 to 31, in English pages 7 through 8; in B/C/S pages 10, you talk about a meeting that you had with Colonel Vukovic and Major Nikolic in June 1995. You say in your statement one of the things that was expressed to you at the meeting was: "Go and tell the Muslims to pack up and leave Srebrenica. We do not want them there." At paragraph 29, and that's English page 7 and B/C/S page 10, you understood, or rather, you referred to the Muslims there, and your understanding was that that referred to the military and the civilian component. What I'd like to know is: In light of what you observed happening here on the 12th of July, whether that was consistent with your meeting with Major Nikolic and Colonel Vukovic back in June?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was very consistent in that the way Colonel Vukovic and Major Nikolic had told us, that they would like all the Muslim elements to leave Srebrenica enclave, is actually what now General Ratko Mladic was telling them, that you'd be ferried out of the enclave to a different place. So it was very consistent with our earlier assessment and also our earlier meeting with Colonel Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I would like to seek a clarification of one answer the witness gave a minute ago. You said, Mr. Kingori, after you gave your assessment of what Mr. Mladic did, you said he was doing the right thing to cool them down and also to tell them that they will be safe on their way out, which actually is an assurance that he was not obliged to obey. The last -- the very last part of this sentence I do not fully understand. Could you explain how this is an assurance that he - and I take it that is Mr. Mladic - was not obliged to obey, to obey to whom? To obey in what respect? It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I mean here is that this is -- this could just be -- have just been mere propaganda, just telling them: You'll be safe, but he doesn't have to ensure that they're safe after that. It is not his -- he is not obliged to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that's at least -- that is an option you consider to be possible, that he said this but did not mean it -- to do it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He didn't have to mean it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed -- I'm also looking at the clock, Mr. Vanderpuye. We're close to the time where we take a break. But could you tell us whether you're on track as far as time is concerned. I think you asked for 90 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I got about an hour in, Mr. President, and I think I -- with any luck, I'll be done in about 15, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please find a suitable moment. I don't know whether that's now or whether that's in a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's just about now, but I do have one clarifying question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Based on Mr. President's question to you, Colonel, seeing that you were there when General Mladic was speaking to the crowd, did you get the sense at the time that what he was saying and doing he meant?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, in some of these utterances, some of these speeches, part of them -- those of us who have been in the military, those who have been in the political world, know that some of them are just political statements. You just want to please people at that particular moment but you don't necessarily have to mean it or follow it through. So according to our own assessment, he just wanted that particular situation to pass and that's it. And we were aware of that and we were following it all the way up to the end -- or knowing that most likely he did not mean whatever he was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a good time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Vanderpuye, I learned, but only a minute ago, that the text and video issue I raised earlier has been discussed and we'll consider how to resolve that and that's relevant for the Defence as well. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, perhaps before the next break you'll be in a position to respond to P18 or would you like to -- or are you not ready yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, we checked, Your Honour. We don't have any objections --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- to have the exhibit introduced into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then P18 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you said you'd need another 15 to 20 minutes. The Chamber grants that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We'll proceed with the video footage from 65 ter 26123. It is ERN V0009016. I'd just like to play it from 02.44.4, as we have on the record, through to 03.51 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. We've stopped at 03.51.7.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, have you -- are you familiar with this particular area that's depicted in this footage, that is, the road?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am. This is the area in Potocari outside DutchBat where the civilians, that is the IDPs, were being led to board the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you in this area on the 13th of July as well as on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you -- or rather, you reference in your statement that there were some separations that occurred. Where in relation to the road depicted here did that occur?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were two separations on record. One of them was when the men were being moved from the women and children, that was the first separation, and being put in a white house and is recorded. The second separation was for the boys who were around 12, 13, 14, up to 16 years who were moving with this group of women and children, and they were being separated and being taken still to the white house. So there are two separations. It was in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Both?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: The first one was where they were -- the IDPs were herded together, where they were put together, the space outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: But this other separation was when they were going to board the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that would have been along this very road?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, along this road.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could show, please, the footage starting at 7.26 and play that through 08.32. All right. We can go ahead and play that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. We've stopped at 08.33.4.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You can see yourself -- I assume you can see yourself in this video-clip; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And a discussion that is occurring regarding the availability of water?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That was the main issue at that particular moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that discussion was about to the extent that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had a problem of water for the IDPs in that the water available from DutchBat was not enough, and we were even requesting for additional water from the BSA which they promised to bring and they later on brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was that water distributed to the refugees at the -- around the compound?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you involved in the distribution of that water?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Definitely, sir. I was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Do you recognise any of the individuals that were depicted in this particular frame, do you recall their names?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Some of them I can't now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If we can play from 8.37 to 8.55.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. We've stopped at 08.55.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Here -- first of all, do you recall this particular event and what you're discussing here?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you're referring to that place that's overcrowded, what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was referring to the white house where all the men who had been removed from the displaced people, that is from the men [sic] and children, had been taken to. That is where they had been put in a place where it was very uncomfortable, very small -- too small for them, and they had no -- there was no freedom, you know. They were huddled together, they were sitting on each other, and it was not comfortable for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt for a moment just for a clarification. Mr. Kingori, you said the white house where all the men who had been removed from the displaced people, that is, from the men and children, perhaps did you mean that -- that the men were separated from the men and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, from women and children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you misspoke. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President -- I'm sorry. Thank you, Judge Fluegge.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In this particular conversation when you were expressing these concerns to these individuals, did you engage in any kind of follow-up action after this discussion concerning the disposition of the men in the white house?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I followed it up with General Ratko Mladic through some BSA soldiers who could speak English, and one of them is very easily identifiable in the video that you have shown. He's a person who could speak, you know, at least good English and is the one who was translating to General Ratko Mladic of my situation; that is, that what they are doing to the men, putting them in one small house, was not good.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could just go for a moment to 06.15 of this video footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I just want to ask you - I'm not going to play it at this point, but we are for the record at 06.15 - do you recognise the individual in the blue vest?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do. This is the man who could be able to speak a bit of English and he is the one who was translating for me with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In your statement you indicate that you at some point went to the white house with General Mladic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to show you is a video clip starting at 09.23 and we'll play that through 09.30. Yeah, we can go ahead and play it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First of all, do you recognise what we see here or what we have seen in this clip?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What we see in the background there is the possessions of all the men who had been taken to the white house. They were being forced to leave whatever they had, the luggage together with the identification passes and all that outside before going into the white house. So this is what you can see in the background.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And this frame we can see you, I believe, and that's at 09.30.7 - is that correct? - on the left side?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I am the one who is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like to play for you now 09.48 through 10.17.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what we see in this frame, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we are seeing here are the belongings that were for the men who had been separated from the women and children before they entered the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let me just -- for the record, we've stopped at 10.17.7. Where is the white house that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the white house is at the back there, that is the one you can see behind there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Behind the gate?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: It is -- yeah, it's somewhere behind the gate because this is the entrance they were going through and then they entered the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is what we see here of the white house on the 13th of July, can you describe what it was like at the time that you went there with General Mladic? Is the condition that we see it here relatively the same or different?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was relatively the same, only that we could be able now to see the people inside because we weren't very close, we could be able to see them inside there, you know, where they were at the top floor. But we could not see the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was there another vantage point into what you could see into the house other than from the angle that we see it now in this particular frame?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There was another view from the -- I think the right side of this gate, that is where you could be able to see it more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you at -- were you able to see from that point on that occasion, that is on the 13th of July, or when you went there with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: On both occasions we could be able to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Your Honours, it's a misquotation. Mr. Vanderpuye said that on the 13th of July they left with General Mladic. That is an incorrect statement because that took place on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 44, line 25 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I do see that and I think it may have been a translation error. I referred to when he went there on the 13th or when we went there with General Mladic, so I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then please rephrase your question and -- so that the witness can answer it. Rephrase it or repeat it --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then if it's a translation error, of course there is no need to rephrase it but --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, when you went there with General Mladic on the 12th of July, was the house and its surroundings in relatively the same condition as it was when you were there on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it was in relatively the same condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a video-clip from the same video starting at 10.22 and play that through 10.56, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We've stopped just now at 10.47.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I wanted to ask you particularly about this frame. You can see some men on a balcony at the white house. Were you able to see this, as we see it now in the footage, at the time that you were there on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was able to see all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
