utterances.text: And were the men similarly on the balcony when you went there on the 12th of July with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. If we can play it out, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have to ask you a couple of questions, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- may I remind you of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're close to your 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You indicated in your statement that you went on the 13th of July to the Srebrenica hospital, that's at paragraph 183, English 40, page 40 and B/C/S page 55. What I wanted to ask you about, specifically, is that you indicated that you assisted MSF to prepare certain lists. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to show you is 65 ter 25624. Do you recognise this document, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was a list of those who were sick in the DutchBat compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is this the list that you helped to compile?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, sir, with MSF.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25624 becomes Exhibit P35, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P35 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness 65 ter 25625.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the list of the people who were working for us, that is for the UN, that we had to give the BSA for them to be allowed the enclave. This included our interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you have -- did you assist to compile this list as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like to tender this as well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25625 becomes Exhibit P36, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P36 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, did you have an opportunity to ask General Mladic about the separation that you saw occurring while you were in the Potocari area concerning the men and the men and boys?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked that question and I was told that the reason why they were being separated is to help them identify those who are soldiers so that they can take them as prisoners of war and maybe later on exchange them with their own prisoners of war held by the Muslim side elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did that relate to also the kids that you saw, 14, 15, and 16-years-olds, as far as you understood?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it did not relate to the kids because for sure the kids were not fighting age, they were not soldiers, so I don't know why they were taking them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Stojanovic, is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We hope so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel. I'm Miodrag Stojanovic. We've already had an opportunity of seeing each other, both in Sarajevo and here, and I'm going to deal with a few topics that are of interest to the Defence. Will you agree with me that you have testified about these events already five times at least before this honourable institution?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that also before the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo you testified about these events at least five times. Some of the testimony was by videolink and other evidence was given directly in the courtrooms of the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think in Sarajevo it's twice, not five.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, may I remind you that we received documents of your testimony in the Bozic et al. case, then in the Trbic case, then the Vukovic Tomic case, then in the Dusko Jevic case, Mendeljev Djuric. Does that refresh your memory to the effect that you testified in more than two cases before the court in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's is several cases, but I think some of them were put together.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the direct examination you spoke about your professional career. However, I would like you to tell the Trial Chamber whether before October 1994, when you first came to the territory of the former Yugoslavia, to Erdut, whether you had any experience with UN peacekeeping missions?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I did not have. That was my first deployment in the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You kept a journal or, let's call them, your personal notes recording daily events that you considered of importance and you did that throughout your stay in Srebrenica; am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This journal or the notes, which were concluded on the 9th of July, 1995, were mentioned for the first time to the Prosecution of the International Criminal Tribunal during the preparations for the Popovic et al. case; am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You also made notes after the 9th of July until the last day of your stay in the enclave, but according to your own statement you destroyed them for your personal safety; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You would also agree with me that after you had left Srebrenica you had a meeting in Zagreb alongside two other UN observers, at which you submitted a report about everything that you had been asked about and about all the events in Srebrenica and that took place on the 24th of July, 1995. Is that correct as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During this briefing to your superior HQ, did you make use of your notes and did you inform them that you had a personal diary that you had been keeping during the reporting period?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, they did not ask about a diary, I did not give them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you say at any point that you had a diary and that you could provide them with the information contained therein? Did you say any to that effect to any of your superiors?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but I gave them a proper account of what happened and it was the truth and they wrote it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please have in e-court document 65 ter 17805, page 1, in both versions; and this is a briefing report of military observers from the Srebrenica enclave compiled on the 24th of July, 1995, in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if it is easier for you we can give you a hard copy of your statement because perhaps you might need it for reference. Now, let's focus our attention on paragraph 2 of this document which reads: "The three UNMOs were from the Netherlands, Ghana, and Kenya. The Dutch officer had kept a detailed daily journal that he offered for future translation and use, the Ghanian had several typewritten sheets, and the Kenyan officer seemed to have no written records." Can you see this?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you this: Was there any reason at that time, during the briefing, for you to avoid disclosing the diary that you kept on a regular basis and that you said nothing about the possibility of using it as refreshing your memory?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, my memory was very sharp, it was -- I had good instincts, I could be able to give a proper account of the whole situation. And if you go further into the para 2 that you have given, you can see where they have written: "From the start of our discussion of the refugee situation, the Kenyan officer took the lead role," meaning I was the one who was leading the whole discussion, I knew everything, so there was no need for anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we're going to go through your 65 ter statement precisely with the aim of finding out how good your memory is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe this is a good time for an instruction to give me. Is this a good time to offer the documents that I'm going to use to be tendered or do I do it at the very end because we are applying different methods with different witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to tender any document at the moment or after having used it and not to wait until the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this guidance, Your Honours. So I tender into evidence document which is the report or debrief of UNMOs from the Srebrenica enclave registered under number 17805 as 65 ter document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There's no objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 17805 becomes Exhibit D15, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D15 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, we're going to use your statement that was admitted into evidence as 65 ter 28118, and I would like to go to page 5 in English, paragraph 18, which is page 7 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think your 65 ter number was not a correct one, but we are talking about P34. Yes. Once a document has been admitted into evidence, it's always better to refer to it by its exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, and we are going to proceed in that way, and I believe we have the correct document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, could you please be kind and take a look at paragraph 18 where you say - and please focus only on the first two sentences which read: "When I met Becirovic or his intelligence officer, most of the time we met at the PTT building. I think it was only once that we met at the Opstina building. As far as I know, there was no local headquarter." I'd like to ask you to tell the Chamber this: To the best of your knowledge, who is this Mr. Becirovic whose name is referred to here?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was Ramiz Becirovic, the Chief of Staff of 28th OG.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the name Ekrem Salihovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am. He was the intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were these two individuals active-duty military officers or were they TO, or Territorial Defence, reservists?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know what I can call them because, for one, I never saw them in uniform. But I know they were in 28th OG. That's what we had been told.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You would agree with me that within the PTT building where you met with them most frequently, there was also a communications centre that was being used by the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There was a small communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the PTT building was also the command post of the 28th Division according to their deployment schedule?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of the 28th Division was whilst you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were always told there was somebody called Naser Oric or a name similar to that, but we did not meet him when we were there. We just heard that he was the one in charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could I ask one clarification. You were asked, Mr. Kingori, whether you were aware that the -- whether there was a -- let me see, whether you knew that the PTT building was also the command post of the 28th Division. You said you didn't know that. Could you tell us whether you observed and whether you were able to observe whether there was any such command post in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were unable to establish any sort of command post. Now, whether there was any command post in that building or any other military installation, other than the communications centre that we could see and that we were holding meetings in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the only thing we could be able to establish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You didn't have access to the remainder of that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, we did not have access to any of the other parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The question I asked you about the names of the people you mentioned was whether you knew, as an UNMO, that during the period while you were there, there was an organised and constituted unit called the 28th Division made up of all its subordinate units and with proper internal organisation?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I can remember and as far as I knew, there was no such an organised division, a military division, as such that was called the 28th OG. It was not as organised as any military division would be because for sure it was very difficult to hold a division in the enclave, a division goes with the necessary support arms, that is like the artillery, tanks, air support, and all that, and that you could not be able to hold in such a small enclave. So militarily -- and somebody as -- you know, like somebody who is from a military background, I know and I knew for sure you could not hold a division in such a place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then I would kindly ask you to take a look together with me at a document which is 65 ter 1D00083. While we are waiting for it to appear in e-court, I'm going to tell you that this is an order issued by the command -- Supreme Command of the armed forces in Sarajevo on the forming of the 8th OG, and the document is dated the 1st of January, 1994. Sir, you can see this document in front of you in which the staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces on the 1st of January, 1994 - that is to say, after the conclusion of the demilitarisation agreement and an agreement on the exclusion of any military elements whatsoever from the demilitarised zone - was nevertheless forming this unit. Please look at paragraph I, subparagraph 1, item (a).

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can see that. It was formed in -- to be in Potocari -- Srebrenica. Yeah, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you look at this document, would you agree that I am right that according to the order of the Supreme Command Staff issued on the 1st of January, 1994, an order was issued under (b) to form the 280th Light Eastern Bosnia Brigade with headquarters in Potocari, 281st Eastern Bosnia Brigade with the HQ in Suceska. Then we need the next page in B/C/S. 282nd Eastern Bosnia Light Brigade with an HQ in Srebrenica, and I'm not going to read more. We have 283rd, 284th Brigade, et cetera, as well as an independent mountain brigade with the headquarters in Srebrenica. Therefore, according to the order that we have here, there are five brigades and there is an independent mountain battalion as an operative unit. Now, according to this document, do you think that that would amend, in any way whatsoever, the observation that you made earlier in terms of there not being any organised unit in Srebrenica or that perhaps you were not able to notice them in view of the area involved?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is actually in paper. For one, I did not get a chance of reading something like this at that particular moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you, Mr. Kingori. Sorry to interrupt you. Do you have any knowledge of this formation of units or military? Do you have any knowledge of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any knowledge of the formation of these units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I wanted to add that according to my big military background and the situation on ground at that particular moment, it was impossible to have such a big force in that particular area, and especially when we talk about a division because it is -- a division is a very big formation, it's the second-highest formation before an army. And a unit goes with its support arms. This is not the way the BSA side was formed. That was an organised military group, that is the BSA. We saw the echelons and support arms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- but here what I'm trying to say is that this could have been on paper, but on ground we could not see something close to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Mr. Stojanovic, we should clearly distinguish between what a witness can tell us what he observed, and of course you can put to him that there's documentary evidence which -- and whether -- which established certain units and whether that causes any doubt on his mind as whether he may have misobserved what really happened on the ground, but that can be done more efficiently than by just putting it briefly to him and this document could perhaps be tendered from the bar table so as to give support to what you put to the witness rather than to read the whole of the document. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours. That was exactly my intention. I was seeking to hear the witness's opinion as well as the question that was put to him before about what he thought that General Mladic had in mind and that motived me to formulate the question in this manner. Maybe, as you say, this is a good time to have this document entered into evidence and we are going to use it at a later stage, and I'm talking about 65 ter document 1D00083.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections. Madam Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes -- I saw you nodding and that's why I said. I always expect the parties, if there's any objection, to raise that spontaneously. Sometimes I would say in the absence of any objections, but even if I do not say that, I expect you to object if there's any objection against admission when the document is tendered. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D83 [sic] becomes Exhibit D16, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D16 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to move to another area. Only one more question relating to the PTT building. Colonel, did you have an opportunity to see that there was a shelter within the building?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you mean a bunker, yes, there was a bunker and we used it. It was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to call again document P34, that's Mr. Kingori's statement given according to 65 ter. We need page 7 in English and 9 in B/C/S. Paragraph 27. Briefly, sir, let's go quickly through this paragraph because I have analysed it extensively. Here you say: "I really do not remember whether it ever happened, because most of the accusations on attacks were coming from the BH, saying that they had been attacked by the BSA, but normally not the other way around, not the BSA complaining about attacks from the BiH. It was, I think, very rare or never occurred." Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now let us take a look together at paragraph 62 of the same statement, page 15 in English and 20, page 20, in B/C/S, paragraph 62, where the Prosecution is instructing you in this statement that what you said, or rather, bringing to your attention that what you said does not correspond entirely to the contents of your diary because this is where meetings with the Army of Republika Srpska during May and June were mentioned, and it was you who personally recorded in this document the complaints from the Serbian side about the military activities of the Bosnian side, and you were being asked why you had never mentioned that before. Now, I would like to tell you that we can refresh your memory about your diary and we can do that, but let me ask you: Do you remember that there had been complaints coming from the Serbian side about the violation of demilitarisation and other issues that were committed or done by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there was some few, and that is why even in the earlier statement you can see I say there were few or none at all, meaning they were there, there are some of them, but not as many as from the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask for a document, 65 ter 04392. Could we please have that in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for it, Your Honours, may I say that this is an operations report that the command of the 28th Division sent to its superior command, namely, the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 30th of June, 1995. This report is signed by the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division, Major Ramiz Becirovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, the first thing I wish to ask you before we focus on this document, and in view of the fact that you have already told us why you think that such a unit did not exist in the enclave, did you know that from the enclave there were several attacks against the territory that was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska outside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We knew these people were connected to other areas where Muslims were, like Zepa, Tuzla, and all that. But just on a clarification of what you said about "inside the enclave," the military organisation there, that you are calling a military organisation, was not there as such. But of course the connections were there and they were known.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you specifically about the military unit that they're dealing with and that was established on the basis of that order. We have before you now a document in which they are reporting to their superior command on what they had done. However, before we move on to that, did you know - and on the basis of the way in which information was collected, as you told us during the first part of your testimony - did you come to learn that a unit inside the enclave, regardless of what its force or strength may have been in organisational structure, had instructions to engage through active combat as many forces of the VRS as possible because of the situation concerning the offensive around Sarajevo. Did you ever receive information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did not receive such information, and also I'm surprised - and maybe that could have come as a surprise - that any military organisation inside Srebrenica could go out there and assist other areas. And what military are we talking about to go out there and assist? You are talking about a handful of civilians with small arms. You are talking about -- all the heavy weapons had been kept in a DutchBat compound, that is the Bravo Company, and that one is evident, and we used to see those arms there, heavy support arms. So in essence, the kind of soldiers you may be talking about are soldiers with small arms, those -- and even their training, I doubt whether it was a proper training, because some of them were just being picked. What I'm trying to tell you, to explain to you, is that there is a difference here - and it needs to be noted - that the BSA actually was an army, was a proper military. Inside the enclave the people you can call -- you are calling an army, in fact these are people with small arms. Yeah, sometimes occasionally we could see or hear about a heavy machine-gun, but nothing beyond that at all. So trying to show like -- they could go there out and support, yes, but in -- at what level of support? At what level? And comparing with the BSA side, then obviously, if this is the intelligence you are using, it obviously maybe meant that you made an overkill when the BSA attacked the enclave, it was an overkill, because these guys were not as heavily armed as you are taking it to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I notice the following. The witness in paragraphs 27 and 62 of his statement stated what was reported to him. Apparently now you are going into detail on whether those reports were right or wrong and what happened on the ground. Before we deal with that with this witness we should first try to find out whether he has any knowledge of what happened there because on his last answer there seems to be a lot of speculation there, that if this would be then you would not expect this, or that would surprise me; that's all speculations, no factual knowledge. Second, the witness made a clear distinction in paragraphs 27 and 62 about any military activity from inside to the outside of the enclave. He said these things were not reported; and if so, on a very minimal scale. Again, if you are putting this to the witness and if you think it's relevant at all, we first have to find out whether the witness has any knowledge about it. He may have misobserved. I'm not saying that it did not happen, not in any way, but let's put questions to the witness on matters he knows and rather not to say: Could it be that you misobserved matters because we have documents which says otherwise. These documents may be very valid evidence, but for the witness to answer questions, we should establish that he has any of such knowledge, that's one; and second, if he makes a clear distinction between reports from what happened from inside, then you should also address that on any further question you ask him. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That is precisely why I'm using this document. It is the document of a unit that says itself that it is a unit within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm going to move step by step, Colonel. This unit within the enclave that you mentioned as the 28th Division, on the 13th of June at the time when you were there says, inter alia, that on the 23rd of June, 1995 - when you were there, in the area of Osmace and in the area of Bijela Stijena - they say themselves that they liquidated seven Chetniks and all with a view to preventing the Army of Republika Srpska from going to the Sarajevo front line as a reinforcement. This is what I'm asking you now: Did you ever have any information about these events, yes or no? And then I shall move on.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will answer you this way. The reports we were getting from the attacks by BSA on the Muslims was coming from the Muslims. Therefore, it means the reports we could have gotten on the Muslims attacking the BSA so -- should have actually come from the BSA. And on this occasion, the BSA never reported any attacks on them, so we had no way of knowing because obviously if the Muslims had attacked, they could not tell us. But the BSA should have informed us in various meetings that we were holding with them. They did not report to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So the answer would be that you had not heard of these events on the 23rd of June; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer is that the report should have come -- could have come from the BSA, they did not report to us so we did not get to know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And for the previous questions, whether you had any knowledge, if you would have said no, that would answered the question as well instead of giving a long explanation as why. If we are interested in further explanations, Mr. Stojanovic will certainly ask you for it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I shall try to put as many questions as possible that would require only yes or no answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 3 of what Ramiz Becirovic says as Chief of Staff of the 28th Division. He is saying to his superior command in Tuzla that his units, with a view to averting enemy forces from the Sarajevo front line and in order to spread them out towards Srebrenica and Zepa, to stretch them, on the 26th of June, while you were in the enclave, they carried out a diversion towards Han Pijesak and Vlasenica and then he says what the areas were, what the actual localities were, and he establishes - I think it's the next page in B/C/S now - and he establishes that on that occasion, according to their estimates, that is to say of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, over 40 Chetniks were killed. And according to unconfirmed information, they sustained losses amounting to 71 soldiers. As a military observer, did you at any point in time, in any of the ways that you described, receive any information about the attack against the village of Visnjica and its torching on the 26th of June, 1995, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I shall move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, again, I -- of course we had only a short opportunity to read through the document. It defines the unit involved in it. But where the operation started, which apparently went well far into territory which was occupied or was under the control of the opposite party, it doesn't say it anywhere. So whether they initiated these operations from within Srebrenica and then went out or whether they were already out and made those operations there, I was unable to find any information on this. And that was the key issue that was put to the witness earlier. I do not find, just reviewing it very quickly, any information about that in this document. As a matter of fact, it does say that the operations were deep inside, as they call it, territory temporarily occupied by the enemy. So it's still -- and you are more or less implicitly blaming Mr. Kingori for not knowing all of this. What he said in his statement was what was reported to him. That was what he limited himself to that, and I think even in the statement we find that what may have happened outside, he has no knowledge of it. So it may well be that it happened. I'm not saying in any way that it did not happen, but let's stick to what this witness can tell us and let's not put the whole of the war history through this witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just in terms of our further questions, in paragraph 1 of this document it states -- it is stated clearly which units actually did that, and it says there that these were soldiers of the 28th Division and they were located in the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa. I'm not going to deal with this any longer, but that was the reason why I used this document. If you allow me, perhaps this would be the right moment to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04392 becomes Exhibit D17, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D17 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Stojanovic, I would not mind if you follow me in my distinction between from where an operation was initiated, that's one, even if you are located in a certain area you may initiate operations from elsewhere; second, you only mentioned paragraph 1 located in the Srebrenica - and it reads - "and Zepa enclaves," which already makes clear that it perhaps could have been from Srebrenica, perhaps from Zepa, or from any other place. I just want you to be very precise on these matters. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If you allow me, Your Honours, just a minute of consultation with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank the Court for their understanding, and I shall proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, could you please clarify your technique of your diary entries. Could you tell me whether you noted down in your diary all the meetings that you had with the parties in and around Srebrenica, that is to say both the Bosnian and the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not have one diary, I had several diaries, and it is written in my report that I had several diaries, one of them which was very important and critical on the BSA side, I had to destroy it for my own safety. But I did not just have one diary -- in fact, it was not a diary as such, it was a book, record, of the meetings and all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to be more specific and I'll ask you to give more specific answers as well. In the notebook that you kept for June 1995, did you record such meetings with any one of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right if I were to say that the conclusions from meetings that you consider to be relevant and important would be included in your daily report and submitted to your headquarters in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you to look at your statement once again, P34. Let's look at that together, the one that you gave according to Rule 65 ter. Page 7 of the English version, 10 in B/C/S, and let us focus our attention on 30 and 31, and Mr. Vanderpuye already dealt with that during his direct examination. In June -- actually, perhaps it would be right and proper if you were to be given the opportunity to read this first. So in June, Colonel, as you say in paragraph 30. In June 1995 you attended a meeting that was held at the Fontana Hotel and where Colonel Vukovic was present. The meeting had been called by Major Nikolic and his team. Do you -- actually, you do remember that there were a few senior officers there, including Colonel Vukovic. First of all, may I ask you the following: Can you tell the Court what is your recollection, who was Colonel Vukovic and do you know which unit he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I knew Colonel Vukovic as a senior BSA officer who was maybe in the headquarters. All I know is that he was a senior BSA officer and he was in charge of that general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So you do not know from the point of view of establishment which unit he belongs to; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "no," you mean that you do not know; is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: When I say "no," Your Honour, I mean I did not know the specific unit that he was leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my understanding, but for the sake of the record I wanted to have it clarified. Now let us look at paragraph 31 of your statement. So this Colonel Vukovic, at that meeting in June 1995, to the best of your recollection says that they do not want the Muslims there, that he can give them safe passage, and if they do not want to leave of their own free will he would kill them. And then you quote his words: "You better leave, and if you don't want to leave willingly we will clear the enclave of you." Will you agree with me that these are extremely serious words and very delicate warnings that you were given on that occasion by Colonel Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, these were very serious issues being and that -- you know, dead-lines being given by Colonel Vukovic. We took them very seriously. We reported the same to the UN system, and later on you see that what he was saying is actually what they did later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, I made an effort to read your notes several times as well as your reports that you submitted to headquarters from June 1995 because you could not specify the date. Nowhere in your reports did I find any of this that would indicate that you conveyed such serious warnings to your superior command. Since the break will take place soon, I would like to ask you kindly to go through your notes. I have them here and could you then please tell us whether I'm right. Also, the UNMO reports that you sent in June 1995, that will be tendered into evidence in this trial. So I'd like to ask you once again, now that I've said all of this to you, are you still of the opinion that you conveyed this serious warning to your headquarters in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, mine is not an opinion. Colonel Vukovic told us this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- the question took one minute, more than one minute, Mr. Stojanovic, where apparently you wanted to ask the witness a very simple question: Did you ever write down in your notes or in any of your reports this threat? And then the answer would be: Yes or no. And that would take us five seconds for the question and now the witness -- did you -- what you said in your statement about if they don't go we'll kill them, did you ever write that down either in your diary or did you report that to any of your superiors in any official report. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wrote it down in my diary, the one I destroyed, and it is supported in the situation report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then the parties are, of course, invited to see whether it's anywhere in those reports. We'll take a break anyhow. Mr. Kingori, could you already follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could you tell us how much time you'd further need for your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, according to my notes and what I planned to ask, I shall try to speed things up by putting simpler questions, although I have an interlocutor who is as verbose as I am, but I think I will be able to finish within the next two hours. I have three video recordings and five documents left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see how it develops. Don't blame the witness for your long questions. If he --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- gives you long answers, it's for you to stop him and to take him back to the question, rather than to say he's long, therefore I'm long as well. That's not an appropriate approach I would say. We'll take a break and we'll resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, if there's anything you would like to raise, please consult with counsel. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if you're ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, with your permission just one digression. We reviewed the transcript and it seems to us that on page 75 [as interpreted], line 7, the last answer given by Mr. Kingori was not recorded. Therefore, I'm going to repeat my question and we can do away with this quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, if I understood you correctly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I do not mind if you have concerns, but I'm at page 72, so what misses at page 75 is not apparent to me yet. Whether you think an answer is missing, please put a short question to the witness and then we'll receive a short answer by him I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's a translation issue, page 70, line 7. You can see that for yourself, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kingori, if I understood your answer correctly, you say that the notes that you destroyed contain the impressions and the information and the threats made by Colonel Vukovic on the meeting of the 25th of June. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I meant was that part of that information is there. But the other information that was there, that was being conveyed to us by the BSA, and also some strategic information concerning the locations of some equipments, and also the use and the attacks on the enclave, some of them were in that notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on now. I'd like to draw your attention again to your statement, P34. Page 11 in English and page 15 in B/C/S, paragraph 46. And we'll just go through this briefly. In examination-in-chief you mentioned the Bandera Triangle. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that that was an integral part of the protected zone of Srebrenica in which the UN observers most often were denied access?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That is very true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that at one point a number of members of DutchBat from the UNPROFOR had even been detained in the Bandera Triangle area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If weapons or ammunition were being supplied to that area, you wouldn't be able to observe that and therefore you wouldn't be able to carry out your mission; am I right if I say that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: You're partly right and partly wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, Mr. Stojanovic. By whom were UN observers denied the right to -- of access and/or even detained, Mr. Kingori?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were denied freedom of movement in the Bandera Triangle by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, can you please tell us, when I say that you were not able to observe the supply of weapons and ammunition, is there any part of the statement that I have just made that is not true?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I said is that when you say the supply of weapons could not have been known by us in that particular area, I said part of what you've said is true and partly not true, in that we -- it is true we could not have known everything in that area that we don't have freedom of movement. At the same time, movement of heavy equipment, movement of arms, could have been seen by other observers. Other observers, I'm talking about the BSA could also have seen and told us about it, so that's why I said it's partly true and partly not true because there were other observers who could have informed us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I received a correct translation, you believe there were military observers, Serb military observers, who could have observed this?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't say "military observers." I said "observers," people who could observe, people who could have seen, and that's why I mentioned the BSA could have seen that. And I will give an example of when an aircraft crashed: A helicopter crashed. We did not see it as military observers, the Muslims did not tell us, but we were told by the BSA about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is my next question. So you did receive information that at one point this area was used as a helicopter pad for supplying necessities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, isn't that in the statement? So if you have any follow-up questions, no problem; but let's then start where the witness stated about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, and this is going to be a question corroborating my own statement. But if you allow me, let me rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, having in mind what you had just said about the information that you had, and knowing what is contained in the documents of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I put it to you that on the 25th of May, 1995, a helicopter was downed, a helicopter which was used to supply provisions and other necessities to the enclave. Is this information correct and did you have it, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the information I have or I got that time was that a helicopter was downed, but whether it was carrying military hardware or not, I do not know. But in my statement you also see I mentioned about Ramiz Becirovic being in that helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you try to investigate this information, to see whose helicopter it was and whether it belonged to the 28th Division or perhaps some other unit of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we tried to investigate, but we could not get more information as to where it belonged, whom it belonged to, and what it could have been carrying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You sought this information from Ramiz Becirovic and other authorities in Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And those were the ones who declined to provide this information to you; am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, on this one my answer is: We were investigating through those people, but at the same time when we sent that report outside to the UN system, the UN headquarters, we expected them to handle it at another level. In fact, that was the essence of such kind of information. So it was not just for our use. Everybody who was in the system was free to investigate and let us know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, what Mr. Stojanovic apparently wants to know is whether when you sought information from Ramiz Becirovic and other authorities in Srebrenica, whether they declined to provide the information you requested. That is the simple question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, when he has talked about Ramiz Becirovic and other authorities in Srebrenica, that's why I'm involving -- I'm involving everybody; that is, Becirovic and his ATG and also the external actors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but did they deny to give you the information you were asking for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did not give us that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That was the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm going to finish this section with one document, then I'll move to another topic. Can we have in e-court 65 ter 25607, pages 4 in both B/C/S and English versions. While we are waiting for it, Your Honours, I'm going to wrap-up this segment with the report, or rather, an introductory note made by the commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, army General Rasim Delic, when he addressed the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina about the reasons and causes of the military fall of Srebrenica in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since this is a rather long document, Mr. Kingori, can we please just take a look at it, specifically page 4, in which the BiH army commander, among other things, says that there is a summary of how many ammunition and pieces of weapons and other pieces of equipment, mortar shells, mortars, communication devices, sniper rifles, and mortar shells were delivered to the Srebrenica enclave, and he says that this amount of supplies had not been received by Gorazde and that the defence of Sarajevo in 1993 used even less equipment and ammunition? In view of your experience as an air force colonel, if you can, would you agree with me and say that I'm right, that this quantity of equipment, weapons, and ammunition and the statement made by the BH army commander to the effect that this big amount was neither possessed by Zepa nor Sarajevo, are you telling me that this was something that was going on in the enclave and that you were unable to observe that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, that's not how you can ask that. You put to the witness a report. Then you start telling him whether this would be what -- what his assessment -- you're asking actually for an expert opinion. And then apparently based on the assumption that it was all delivered, then you ask the witness whether it's reasonable that he could have missed it, yes or no. That's, first of all, three questions; you should split them up. So please take it in an orderly manner this matter and ask questions, of course, primarily -- although you, of course, you may put something to a witness if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll go step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: First, Mr. Kingori, my question is: Did you and your colleagues from the UN observer mission have any information about the supply of these weapons and equipment, et cetera, as listed here by the BH army commander, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: No, we did not have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: Bearing in mind your professional experience, to which you referred in examination-in-chief when you answered Mr. Vanderpuye's questions, was this quantity that you see before you a respectable one consisting of weapons and ammunition, as qualified by the army General Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand what is meant by "respectable" in the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And apart from that, Mr. Stojanovic, it says: "Until the time of the accident in May, we managed to supply the following to Srebrenica (without Zepa)." Would that mean that in order to give an assessment if at all possible, whether this was reasonable supplies for a small unit or a larger unit, and apparently that does not appear in your question yet, but that you wouldn't have to know starting at what date? Was this since 1992, was this since 1993, was this until -- by the way, may I take it, although it doesn't say so, and the witness would not know, that May most likely is until May 1995, at least I could guess that that is it. And then second, the witness arrived after that. So these are at least four or five uncertainties which have to be clarified because you could even ask this question to the witness apart from whether the question itself is clear. So please take it in an orderly manner and try to elicit the evidence you are seeking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honours. I'll try to separate my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, the quantity, or rather, quantities of equipment, ammunition, and weapons that you see before you in this document, page 4, according to your knowledge, would that quantity be sufficient to arm a unit equal to a brigade in strength?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's difficult for me to answer this because I don't know from when and whether it was supplied at one time, just once, or is a continuous supply? Because the way they are saying here is: "Until the time of accident in May ..." And the war started much earlier, I think it started in 1991, so it's difficult for me to answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please move on, Mr. Stojanovic. It might also depend on how heavy the smokers are which have to consume the cigarettes which are on this list. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honours. I will endeavour to make only one more digression from this document, and after that I would seek this document to be tendered in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But before that, please look at page 3 of this document in both versions where it says that: "The worst accident occurred on the 7th of May, 1995, when a helicopter was destroyed right above its destination ... on which occasion the helicopter crew was killed and nine of twenty-two passengers, among whom were three doctors ... who were recruited for the needs of the 28th Division." Now my question is: Is this information consistent with the information that you mentioned some time ago about the shooting down of a helicopter?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's difficult for me to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you any further questions about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps this is a good opportunity to tender this document, 65 ter 25607, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25607 becomes Exhibit D18, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D18 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, allow me to move to another topic now and we'll try to be more speedy. On the 9th of July you decided for personal safety reasons --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your indulgence, is it possible for me to have a brief consultation with my client?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, on the 9th of July, according to your statement, you decided for personal safety reasons to leave Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to take a look at your document P34 -- actually, your statement, paragraph 104. In English it's page 23, B/C/S 32. In the statement that you gave that was admitted into evidence, you said, inter alia, that you wanted to have a meeting with the deputy mayor so that he can give us permission to leave the PTT building. "It may look a bit funny that we were asking for permission, but we felt intimidated by the presence of some armed BiH soldiers out of the building moving around." Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What I would like to ask you about this segment of your testimony is the following. At that specific moment, that is to say on the 9th of July -- and if you can give an estimate to the Court, approximately at what time you had this conversation or meeting with the deputy mayor?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first meeting was slightly after 12.00, so it could have been about 1300 hours, somewhere there, which he declined to give us the permission to leave the PTT building. And later on we had another meeting with him later around -- just some minutes to 6.00, of which he agreed to let us leave PTT.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, at that point in time, on the 9th, either during the first or the second meeting, did you have information that on the previous day at 1450 hours, that is, the 8th of July, while UNPROFOR was withdrawing from Foxtrot observation post, one member of the BH army killed one of the members of the APC crew, a member of the Dutch Battalion?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that precisely the cause of your concern, as a result of which you sought permission from the representative of the local authorities to leave Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it was not. That was not the reason why we had to seek permission, and the reason was we saw those armed personnel outside there, and there were a lot of people, a lot of IDPs who were outside the main entrance. And thirdly, we did not want to leave like we are running away because we had stayed with them for a long time and we had already seen a tank positioned at a certain location about 2 kilometres away to the right, and we knew that that was a possible assault on the area. So we wanted to leave, and peacefully too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I shall stop you there, with all due respect. I shall interrupt you with all due respect, because the question was whether that was the reason and the answer is no and I have to move on. Please, now let us look together at 04005, that's a 65 ter number, let's look at that together in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, while we're waiting for the document to appear, let me say that it was signed by Osman Suljic on the 9th of July, 1995, and that corresponds to what Mr. Kingori was saying a moment ago. This is a document that the Presidency of the Srebrenica municipality is sending to the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, and to the commander of the RBH army, army General Rasim Delic, who we mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And it says here, inter alia, in line 5 from the bottom that: "Urgently, at the level of state and military organs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina a meeting with the Serb aggressor side be held as expeditiously as possible with the aim of finding a possibility to opening a corridor for the population to move to the nearest free territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina under the control of international factors." This is my question to you now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is my question to you: On that day, on the 9th, dramatic things were already underway. Did you have information to the effect that the civilian leadership of the enclave of Srebrenica was asking for a meeting with the Serb side in order to find the possibility of opening a corridor for the population to move out, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: No, we were not aware of that, and this meeting is being recorded later in the day, 1900 hours, and we had already left PTT.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you were in Potocari at the facilities of DutchBat; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the following information from the sources that you mentioned in your direct examination, namely, that the leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina - as we've heard here - Alija Izetbegovic and Hasan Muratovic, refused the possibility of opening a corridor and having the population move out; did you receive that information?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I shall move on, Your Honours. This may be the right moment for me to ask you to have this document admitted into evidence, 65 ter 04005, that's the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04005 becomes Exhibit D19, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D19 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Stojanovic, before you proceed there are a few smaller procedural matters which I would like to deal with before we adjourn. If you have one or two or three minutes for your next questions, that's okay; but if you have other plans, then I'd rather already excuse the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Honours, I would opt for the second possibility then, Your Honour. Could I please ask how much time I have left tomorrow so that I reorganise myself and deal with matters as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we'll check. You said you would need another two hours and you expected to finish within two hours. We'll ask the Registry for detailed information. We'll let you know. Then, Mr. Kingori, we will soon adjourn for the day but have to deal with a few other matters. I would like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in any other way with whomever about your testimony, whether it's testimony already given or testimony still to be given tomorrow, and we expect to conclude your -- hearing your evidence tomorrow. Could you please follow the usher, and we would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There were a few matters left. Let me start with one about the hearings this week. Earlier this week the Defence requested that the Chamber consider sitting for shorter periods for the remainder of this week, and that request is at transcript page 918. After considering the Defence request and taking into consideration that there is not enough time to receive medical information, the Chamber nonetheless informs the parties that for the two remaining days this week, that is, Thursday and Friday, Friday, the 20th of July, the court sessions will be shortened to no more than one hour of sitting time, but this also means that the breaks will be shortened to 20 minutes. Therefore, we'll sit until approximately 10.00, have then a break until 10.20; then continue until 11.20, then resume after a break at 11.40 until 12.40; and then the final session will begin at approximately 1.00 p.m. and will last for 45 minutes, until 1.45 p.m., the regular end time of a morning court hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Groome, you asked to be allowed to make short submissions on proposed -- on a proposal with how to deal with adjudicated facts and agreed facts, and also something about the reference to 65 ter numbers. You have the next nine minutes to make such submissions. If you cannot finish, we'll try to find more time tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I do that, though, in connection with what Your Honours have just said, the Prosecution have been watching the amount of time that we were using this week and had considered the possibility of discussing with the Defence the conversion of RM255 from my viva voce to a 92 ter witness. There is a good statement that we could use. Could I ask the Chamber, if Mr. Lukic does agree to such conversion, would the Chamber entertain an oral application to take this witness's evidence 92 ter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We would entertain such an oral application.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I first address you on adjudicated facts. Your Honours, it is the Prosecution's intention to incorporate into its case comprehensive reliance on the adjudicated facts of other Chambers, which this Chamber has taken judicial notice of. While doing so permits this trial to benefit from the work and reliable factual findings of other Trial Chambers, the Prosecution must be cautious of when and how it relies on them, to ensure that we do so appropriately and we do so in a way that should the fact be challenged at some time in the future, the Prosecution is in a position to demonstrate to this Chamber, or the Appeals Chamber, what evidence it did not adduce in reliance on a particular fact. With respect to witnesses who do testify, the Prosecution is proposing that it follows a procedure similar to what I did with Mr. Harland and what Mr. Vanderpuye did with Mr. Kingori; that is, where the Prosecution believes it can appropriately not adduce evidence in reliance on an adjudicated fact or facts, it will make a brief statement that it is doing so; where knowledge of these facts is necessary to contextualise the witness's evidence which is led in court, the Prosecution will briefly summarise the facts so that the Chamber and the Defence can better understand the witness's evidence. This practice may assist the Chamber in the future. Should a particular fact be challenged, the Chamber can identify at least some of the evidence the Prosecution did not adduce in reliance on the adjudicated fact. Such practice will also serve to notify the Defence, should they wish to challenge particular facts, which witnesses the Prosecution believes are capable of providing evidence relevant to these facts. The Prosecution considers that the Defence, knowing such, will be placed in a better position to adduce evidence pursuant to Rule 90(H), which may serve to challenge that fact. Your Honour, that concludes my observations or submission on adjudicated facts. I don't expect any response from the Defence or the Chamber. I just wanted to make these submissions in the hopes that over the course of the recess they might be considered; and if the Chamber disagrees with such a procedure, they can make that note to the Chamber and we'll of course adapt our procedures accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course the Chamber would appreciate if it would know the position of the Defence on it when we consider this, not necessarily to be given now, Mr. Lukic, but soon in an appropriate format. Then we'll consider the matter and I think you also wanted to make a proposal on agreed facts --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Agreed facts. Yes, Your Honour. Your Honours pointed out, I believe it was on Monday, that if the Prosecution agreed with a Defence assertion to Mr. Harland, that no peacekeepers were killed while held by the VRS, it was unnecessary to explore this topic with the witness. I have a small suggestion regarding how this trial process may be made more efficient through greater reliance on agreed facts. First, what I propose now would have no impact on the need for the Prosecution and Defence to meet regularly to identify matters of fact and law for which there is no dispute between the parties and can appropriately be the subject of an agreement. This process should continue and the Prosecution always remains available for discussions with the Mladic Defence to identify such facts. The Defence should not assume that simply because a fact is perceived as unfavourable to the Prosecution's case, the Prosecution will not enter into an agreement. If the Prosecution believes that a particular fact is truthful, accurate, and beyond reasonable dispute, the Prosecution will give careful consideration to stipulating to its accuracy and truthfulness. The Prosecution proposal relates to the situation that arose on -- earlier this week with respect to whether peacekeepers had been killed, and I would like to make the following three points. First, there may be numerous occasions over the course of this trial that a line of inquiry by the Defence may elicit evidence of facts which the Prosecution does not dispute. I suspect that it may be more frequent occurrence than its converse. I also appreciate that the Mladic Defence may only develop its final lines of questioning after hearing a Prosecution witness give its direct evidence. It is my intention to be present at all court hearings, and I undertake to make myself and my colleagues available before court and during breaks to discuss the possibility of agreeing to any facts the Defence may wish to put to a Prosecution witness. It may be a fact such as we heard in Mr. Harland's evidence, it may be the fact that a witness said a particular thing in a previous statement. We will also endeavour to be proactive in that if a line of inquiry commences which we are prepared to agree to, we will rise to inform the Defence and the Chamber that the Prosecution agrees to the facts being put to the witness. Second, in order to make effective use of agreed facts, it is necessary to be able to find them easily in the trial record. If measures are not taken to make them readily searchable, they are likely to be difficult to find and, hence, rely on at a later stage of the trial. To this end, whenever the Prosecution does agree to a particular fact during the course of an examination, the Prosecution will use the word "stipulate" or a variation of it. This word is defined in Black's Law Dictionary as: "An agreement between attorneys that concerns business before a court and is designed to simplify or shorten litigation." This word is unlikely to appear in the record related to other matters and will allow everyone working on this case to use the search feature of LiveNote to efficiently find each of these agreements. Finally, I would like to make clear the basis upon which the Prosecution would agree to a fact. We will apply a two-fold criteria. First, is the fact a matter of dispute or a matter of consequence to the adjudication of this indictment? If it is not, then the Prosecution will consider whether agreement is appropriate. Second, are we able to verify that the proposed fact is, in fact, accurate and reliable? It would be an unfortunate occurrence which could possibly undermine confidence in these proceedings if erroneous facts were allowed to infiltrate the careful and deliberate fact-finding process simply because they were not of apparent consequence to an adjudication of the indictment. Your Honour, that's my submission on agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. We might not find time to also deal with 65 ter numbers, where I understood you would like to make submissions as well. We'll find soon a moment for that. Mr. Lukic, please consider what Mr. Groome said, as the Chamber will do. And if you want to present your position on short notice, then we would consider that as well in deciding on whether or not we would adopt and follow these suggestions made by Mr. Groome. We adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 19th of July, in this same courtroom, I.
